title: Robinhood: The Private to Public Market Bridge
snippet: By: Nicholas Grous, Director of Research, Consumer Internet & Fintech
content_html:
By: Nicholas Grous, Director of Research, Consumer Internet & Fintech

Robinhood Securities is now approved to serve as an underwriter for initial public offerings (IPOs).

That may sound like a narrow capital markets update, but I think it is much bigger than that. Robinhood is no longer just the app where retail investors buy stocks after companies are public. It is building toward a full-stack private-to-public capital markets platform.

The market structure backdrop matters.

Thanks for reading! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

Today, companies are staying private for longer. Jay Ritter’s IPO data suggests that the number of domestically listed companies on US exchanges today is nearly half its peak in the mid-1990s.

Because companies are staying private longer, more value creation is occurring before retail investors get access. So retail investors face a structural access problem: fewer public companies, later IPOs, and a larger share of growth captured in private markets.

Robinhood appears to be attacking that problem across the full lifecycle.

First, private market access. Robinhood Ventures Fund I gives public investors exposure to private companies through a listed vehicle. Fund I is now live, and Robinhood describes the product as a way to let investors get exposure to companies that often stay private for longer. Strategically, Robinhood is creating a retail-facing distribution layer for private companies before they go public.

Second, IPO Access. Robinhood launched IPO Access to let customers request shares at the IPO price as a company becomes available to the public. Historically, Robinhood participated when investment banks invited it into IPO distribution, and its own support page notes that it was “not an underwriter” but instead received allocations from investment banks to offer to customers through IPO Access.

That model already helped move retail closer to the IPO process. Historically, retail investors have received only a small slice of IPO allocations. In large-cap IPOs, retail has received about 5-10% of shares on offer.

But the trend is moving toward larger retail participation. Robinhood’s own IPO pushed that boundary, with the company planning to allocate 20-35% of shares to retail investors. SpaceX is continuing that trend, with 20% of its IPO allocated to retail investors in one of the most anticipated IPOs in recent history.

If retail investors today have the opportunity to participate in high-profile IPOs at the IPO price, Robinhood deserves much of the credit. Its IPO Access program has helped expand retail participation and demonstrated that individual investors could play a meaningful role in public offerings.

Now comes the third layer: underwriting.

This is the missing piece. As an underwriter, Robinhood can move from participating in IPO distribution to helping shape the issuer relationship itself. That changes the strategic value proposition for companies.

An IPO is not just a financing event. It is also the creation of a shareholder base. For consumer companies, fintech companies, AI companies, crypto companies, marketplaces, and other community-driven businesses, retail ownership can be an important part of the go-to-market strategy. These companies don’t just want investors to show up after the first trade. They want customers, users, developers, and fans who are long-term believers in the company’s vision involved from the very beginning.

That is where Robinhood could be differentiated. It has private-market distribution through Robinhood Ventures, IPO price access through IPO Access, and a large retail investor base that companies may want to tap into directly. With more than 27.7 million funded customers as of May 31 and newly acquired underwriting capabilities, Robinhood is emerging as a formidable capital markets platform that could meaningfully expand retail investors’ access to some of the world’s most valuable private and public companies.

The flywheel is important.

If Robinhood invests in or provides exposure to a private company through Ventures, it can help build early retail awareness before the IPO. If that company eventually goes public, Robinhood can help convert that awareness into IPO demand through IPO Access. As an underwriter, Robinhood can then offer the issuer a more integrated path: private market exposure, retail education, IPO allocation, and post-listing liquidity on the same platform.

For companies, that could become a reason to choose Robinhood earlier in the lifecycle. A venture investment from Robinhood is not just capital. It can be an on-ramp to a future retail shareholder base. Choosing Robinhood as an underwriter is not just about execution. It’s distribution, brand alignment, and building a public-market community from day one.

That is the bigger shift. Robinhood is positioning itself as more than a brokerage. It is building a private-to-public ownership platform that connects companies and retail investors across multiple stages of the capital lifecycle.

Private exposure. IPO access. IPO underwriting. Public trading.

That is a very different Robinhood from the one the market may be underwriting today.
